lead: A machine learning project starts before any algorithm is chosen. It starts with a promise: a task, a way to score it, and data that can teach it. When those three are stated, the problem is well posed and a learning system can be designed. The design turns the promise into a pipeline: collect data, choose features, pick a hypothesis space and algorithm, measure performance, then deploy. Banks use this to decide loan risk; IRCTC uses it to predict waitlist clearance; a phone keypad uses it to suggest the next word. The same discipline applies to each.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for features and labels, and Chapter 1.2 for learning types.

sections.h3: Well-posed means T, P and E

blocks.text: Well-posed learning problem. A learning problem is well posed when three parts are fixed. T is the task: the exact mapping from inputs to outputs that the system must perform. P is the performance measure: a number computed on cases not used in training. E is the experience: the data, labels, rewards or interactions available for learning. Write the triple as (T, P, E).

items: T answers: what is the input, and what is the output?
P answers: how is success scored, and on which cases?
E answers: what past cases or feedback are available?

blocks.text: A fourth check is the data source. Who recorded the data? Is it labelled? Is it from the same population as deployment? A problem with T and P but no honest E is not solvable; it is only a wish. For example, 'predict loan default' is not well posed until P (accuracy? recall? cost?) and E (5000 past loans with repayment outcomes) are fixed. A clear data source makes the problem testable.

items: Write T, P, E and the data source in one page; fix the unit of P, such as accuracy or rupees of cost.
Collect data from the deployment population; record labels or rewards with the same definition used at prediction time.
Prepare data: repair errors, handle missing values, and split into training, validation and test sets before any feature choice.
Choose a representation: define the feature vector x and label y; a feature is a measurable input property.
Choose a hypothesis space H: lines, trees, rules or networks that the learner may return.
Choose a learning algorithm: the procedure that searches H using E.
Train on the training set, tune on validation with P, and report the test score once.
Deploy, monitor inputs and errors, and retrain when the population changes.

blocks.where: h* is the chosen hypothesis; H is the hypothesis space, the set of candidate models; P(h) is the validation performance of hypothesis h.

blocks.text: Two failure points deserve a check. First, choose P before seeing results, otherwise the score can be chosen to flatter the model. Second, keep test data untouched; leakage makes P optimistic. Chapter 1.4 lists the common data and generalization failures. Full evaluation metrics come in Unit 2, Regression and Model Evaluation.
Three views help when choosing a representation.

items: Geometric view: each example is a point in feature space; the model is a boundary, line or curve that separates or fits the points.
Probabilistic view: the model estimates P(y | x), the probability of label y given features x; this also gives uncertainty.
Logical view: the model is a rule, such as 'if income is high and debt is low then repay'; the rule is true or false for each example.

blocks.text: Learning is search over hypotheses. The hypothesis space H is the set of all models the algorithm may return. E supplies the evidence, and P scores each candidate. With many features, H can be huge or infinite. The algorithm cannot test every model, so it uses a search strategy and an inductive bias. Chapter 1.6 shows Find-S and version spaces for concept learning. Chapter 1.7 explains why bias is necessary for generalization. The same search view applies to decision trees, neural networks and support vector machines later in the course.

figure.caption: The flow from a stated task and data to a deployed model. Notice that performance is measured before deployment, not after.

spec.title: Designing a learning system
spec.aria: A design flow from task T and data E through representation and algorithm to performance P and a deployed model.

examples.question: A bank has 5000 past loan records. 500 borrowers defaulted; 4500 repaid. The bank first states: T = predict repay or default at application; P = accuracy; E = the 5000 labelled records. (a) Compute the accuracy of a model that always predicts repay. (b) Compute its recall for the default class. (c) If a missed default costs ₹1,00,000 and a wrongly rejected good loan costs ₹5,000, compute the total cost of this always-repay model. (d) Explain why the problem is not well designed and state one better P.
steps: Total records N = 5000. Defaulters D = 500. Repayers R = 5000 - 500 = 4500.
Always-repay predicts repay for all 5000 records. Correct predictions = 4500. Accuracy = 4500 / 5000 = 0.90 = 90%.
Take default as the positive class. True positives TP = 0; false negatives FN = 500. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 0 / 500 = 0.0.
The score P hides the default class: 90% accuracy comes from the majority class, and recall is 0. A better P is recall on defaults at a fixed false-positive budget, or expected rupee cost.
examples.answer: The always-repay model has accuracy 0.90 (90%), recall 0.0 for default, and cost ₹5,00,00,000; the problem is not well posed for the bank until P targets default detection or cost.
examples.check:
N = 5000
D = 500
R = N - D
correct = R
acc = correct / N
recall = 0 / D
miss_cost = 100000
false_reject_cost = 5000
missed = D
false_rejects = 0
cost = missed * miss_cost + false_rejects * false_reject_cost
print(correct)
print(N)
print(acc)
print(recall)
print(cost)

traps: Stating only the task T and forgetting the performance measure P and the experience E. A task alone is not a learning problem.
Using accuracy on imbalanced data as the only performance measure. A trivial majority-class rule can look strong while the rare class is never found.
Confusing E with the whole database. E is the experience actually available for learning, with its labels and data source checked.
Choosing an algorithm before fixing the representation and the measure. The score can then be picked to suit the model instead of the goal.

quiz.q: Define T, P and E in a well-posed learning problem.
quiz.a: T is the task: the input-output mapping to be learned. P is the performance measure on unseen cases. E is the experience: data, labels, rewards or interactions used for learning.

quiz.q: Why is accuracy a poor only measure for 500 defaulters out of 5000 loans?
quiz.a: The majority class is 4500/5000 = 90%. A model that always predicts repay gets 90% accuracy but finds zero defaulters. Accuracy hides the rare, costly class.

quiz.q: A dataset has 2000 records: 200 positive and 1800 negative. A model predicts negative for all. Compute accuracy and recall for the positive class.
A team states T and E but not P. Give two ways the design can fail.
quiz.a: Models cannot be compared on a common scale, so the wrong model may be deployed. A trivial model may be accepted because no measure exposes its failure. The team also cannot decide when performance is good enough.

quiz.q: A missed default costs ₹1,00,000. There are 500 defaults, and a model misses all of them with no false rejects. What is the cost?
Which view gives P(y | x) directly, and why is that useful for a loan officer?
quiz.a: The probabilistic view gives P(y | x), the probability of default given the applicant's features. The officer can set a risk threshold instead of accepting only a hard yes or no.

quiz.q: Why split data into training and test sets before choosing features?
quiz.a: The test set must mimic unseen cases. If features are chosen after looking at the test set, information leaks and the measured performance is optimistic.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the design cycle becomes MLOps when deployment and monitoring are automated. Data-centric AI focuses on data quality, labelling and coverage rather than model choice alone. Model cards and datasheets document intended use and data sources. Search for 'MLOps pipeline', 'data-centric machine learning' and 'model cards' to go further.
